screens.title: Orchestrating Deployments with AWS CodeDeploy
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn why CodeDeploy is more than a file mover. CodeDeploy is an orchestration engine that coordinates releases across different compute platforms, enforces lifecycle scripts, and integrates automated rollbacks and alarms so you can deploy with confidence. We'll ground the ideas in concrete artifacts: applications, deployment groups, deployment configurations, AppSpec lifecycle hooks, and deployment strategies such as blue/green and canary. You will see the practical tradeoffs: when you need a rapid AllAtOnce push, when to prefer canary testing for live user exposure, and when blue/green is essential to achieve near-zero downtime and instant rollback. We will also cover how to author and validate AppSpec files and how to diagnose failures by inspecting CodeDeploy agent logs and CloudWatch. By the end you should be able to design a deployment group, choose a deployment configuration for your risk profile, and set up alarms and ValidateService hooks that catch real problems before they reach users. Consider what an acceptable rollback trigger looks like for your service and how tests and alarms can be combined to protect production.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Skills in Action
screens.narratorSegment: This lesson emphasizes practical application. You will set up a CodeDeploy application and create a deployment group that targets instances by tag or Auto Scaling group. You will author an AppSpec file that copies files, runs preinstall and validate scripts, and triggers rollback on failures. You will also configure CloudWatch alarms tied to HTTP 5XX rates or latency and link those alarms to CodeDeploy for automatic rollback in blue/green or canary flows. When troubleshooting, you will practice reading the CodeDeploy deployment timeline to identify which hook failed and then examine the CodeDeploy agent logs and script outputs on the instance to find the root cause. Keep in mind that developing robust ValidateService scripts and correct IAM permissions are the two most common practical blockers. This objective helps you close that gap.

screens.title: What is AWS CodeDeploy?
screens.narratorSegment: AWS CodeDeploy is a managed service that automates deploying application revisions to a range of compute targets. Think of CodeDeploy as the orchestration layer between your build artifacts and the running instances or services. It stores a revision (for example a zip bundle in S3), maps that revision to an application, and then executes a deployment to a defined set of targets described by a deployment group. In practice, CodeDeploy handles file transfer, lifecycle hooks, traffic shifting for blue/green or canary strategies, and integrates with CloudWatch for automated rollback triggers. A concrete example is deploying a static website bundle to two EC2 instances: CodeDeploy will copy files, run pre- and post-install scripts, and use ValidateService to check the site responds. A common misconception is to treat CodeDeploy only as a file copier; instead, you should treat it as an execution engine that runs your scripts and enforces success criteria. That means well-written lifecycle scripts and correct IAM permissions are critical. Key benefits include repeatability, visibility via the deployment timeline, and safe rollback mechanisms. As you design pipelines, place CodeDeploy after your artifact storage step and before verification and post-deploy tests so it can execute validation hooks and trigger rollbacks when needed. What minimal validation would you include for your next deployment?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: CodeDeploy automates and orchestrates deployments, runs lifecycle hooks, and enables traffic shifts and rollbacks across multiple compute platforms.

content.html:
Core Concept What is CodeDeploy?
CodeDeploy in one sentence
A managed orchestration service that deploys revisions to EC2, ECS, Lambda, and on-premises targets while running lifecycle hooks and coordinating traffic shifts.
Repeatable deployments with a revision and deployment history.
Lifecycle hooks to validate, start, and clean up during deployments.
Integration with CloudWatch for alarms and automatic rollback triggers.
Key Takeaway

Treat CodeDeploy as an execution engine: focus on robust hooks and monitoring, not just file transfer.

Concrete example
Deploy a static web bundle from S3 to EC2 instances. AppSpec copies files, AfterInstall starts the web server, ValidateService checks the HTTP endpoint, and CodeDeploy will rollback if validation fails.
Common misconception
Do not assume CodeDeploy fixes broken application scripts. If your lifecycle scripts fail or lack permissions, the deployment will fail and rollback may be triggered.
Try this: name one lifecycle check you would add to ValidateService to ensure user-facing functionality works.

screens.title: Applications and Deployment Groups
screens.narratorSegment: At the center of CodeDeploy are two simple concepts: applications and deployment groups. An application is a logical container for your deployment artifacts and configuration. It doesn’t run code itself; instead it groups the deployment groups and the revision history for a particular product or service. A deployment group is where the practical action happens: it defines the set of compute targets that will receive a revision, the deployment configuration to control concurrency, and optional load balancer settings for traffic shifting. Targets are identified differently depending on the platform: EC2/on-premises targets can be selected by instance tags, Auto Scaling group names, or explicit instance IDs; ECS uses a cluster and service; Lambda uses the function name. For example, you might create a deployment group that targets instances tagged Environment:Blue for an in-place update, or create a blue/green group that uses two target groups on an ALB for traffic shifting. A common error is mis-scoping a deployment group: if tags are wrong or IAM roles lack required permissions, CodeDeploy will not find or update targets. The immediate design question is how to scope groups so deployments are predictable and reversible. Think about which selection method — tags, ASG, or explicit IDs — best fits your operational workflow and scaling model.

keyIdea.title: Mapping
keyIdea.text: Applications group configuration; deployment groups target compute resources and control deployment behavior including load balancer integration.

content.html:
Definition
Applications & Deployment Groups
How CodeDeploy scopes where and how your revisions land.
Deployment Group Components
  • Target selection method: EC2 tags, Auto Scaling group, instance IDs, ECS cluster/service, or Lambda function.
  • Deployment configuration: controls concurrency and pace (AllAtOnce, OneAtATime, HalfAtATime).
  • Load balancer settings: for blue/green, specify target groups and listener actions for traffic shift.
  • Service role: IAM role allowing CodeDeploy to interact with the compute platform and load balancers.
Key Takeaway

Scope deployment groups carefully: selection method and IAM permissions determine whether targets are found and updated.

Concrete scenario
Create a deployment group that targets an Auto Scaling group named WebASG. Attach the ALB and BlueTargetGroup as the original target. For blue/green, configure a GreenTargetGroup for replacement instances so CodeDeploy can shift traffic using the ALB.
Common mistake
Using instance IDs for targets in a dynamic Auto Scaling environment. When instances scale, a tag or Auto Scaling group selection keeps targeting up to date.

screens.title: Deployment Configurations
screens.narratorSegment: Deployment configurations determine how many targets are updated simultaneously during a deployment. Choosing the right one balances speed with risk and rollback complexity. The AllAtOnce option updates all targets at the same time. It is fast but risky: a faulty release affects all users immediately. OneAtATime serializes updates so only one instance is changed and validated at a time; this is slow but reduces blast radius and makes troubleshooting simpler. HalfAtATime updates roughly half of instances concurrently, giving a middle ground between speed and safety. When designing your deployment, map your risk tolerance, statefulness, and session handling to a configuration. Stateful services with sticky sessions or long-lived connections may require serial updates or sticky-aware load balancer configurations. For example, an A P I behind an ALB might tolerate HalfAtATime if you have health checks and autoscaling; a database migration that adds incompatible changes would require a OneAtATime or blue/green approach. A frequent misconception is to treat deployment configuration as the only safety control; it must be combined with lifecycle hooks and health checks for meaningful protection. Always test your chosen configuration in a staging environment and measure rollback time for each option so you can quantify the cost of a failed release.

keyIdea.title: Concurrency
keyIdea.text: Deployment configurations control update concurrency and should match your application's tolerance for risk and downtime.

content.html:
Comparison
Deployment Configurations
AllAtOnce
Fastest; updates every target simultaneously. Use for non-critical or quickly reversible changes.
OneAtATime
Safest; updates one target at a time. Use for stateful services or risky migrations.
HalfAtATime
Balanced speed and safety; updates groups of targets concurrently.
Example decision
If you have 10 stateless web servers behind an ALB with health checks, HalfAtATime or OneAtATime will reduce risk of widespread failure while keeping reasonable deployment time.
Checklist before choosing
  • Is the service stateful or stateless?
  • Are client sessions sticky or short-lived?
  • How long does a rollback take?
  • Do you have robust health checks and monitoring?
Pro tip: Combine a conservative deployment configuration with ValidateService checks and CloudWatch alarms to automate safe rollbacks.

screens.title: Blue/Green Deployments
screens.narratorSegment: Blue/green deployments isolate the new version in a separate environment, the green environment, while the current production version continues to serve traffic in blue. The process begins by provisioning or identifying replacement targets in the green environment. CodeDeploy deploys the new revision to green and runs all lifecycle hooks, including ValidateService. Once validation passes, you shift traffic from blue to green via the load balancer. If any validation or CloudWatch alarm triggers a failure, you can immediately shift traffic back to blue. For EC2 this often means launching new instances and registering them in the green target group; for ECS it creates a new task set; for Lambda it publishes a new function version and shifts alias routing. Concrete example: with an ALB, configure BlueTargetGroup and GreenTargetGroup, deploy v2 to green, and set the ALB listener to route to green after successful validation. A common mistake is assuming immediate termination of blue instances; unless you explicitly configure termination, retain blue until you're confident. Also, ensure the AppSpec ValidateService hook performs real end-to-end checks so the traffic shift is based on meaningful verification. After a successful shift, you may optionally terminate the blue instances to reclaim resources. What health checks will you run before rerouting traffic?

keyIdea.title: Blue/Green
keyIdea.text: Deploy to a separate green environment, validate it, then shift traffic to achieve near-zero downtime and quick rollback capability.

content.html:
Process Flow
Blue/Green Deployment Steps
1. Provision green
New instances, task set, or function version.
2. Deploy & run hooks
Install, start, and validate scripts run in green.
3. Verify health
Run end-to-end checks and watch CloudWatch alarms.
4. Shift traffic
Switch ALB listener or update Lambda alias to route to green.
Example: Using an ALB with BlueTargetGroup and GreenTargetGroup, deploy v2 to the green target group, validate with health checks and integration tests, then reroute the listener. If alarms trip, reroute back to blue immediately.
Why it matters
Blue/green minimizes user impact and provides an instant fallback to the previously known good environment. It is ideal for high-availability services and schema-incompatible changes.
Common mistake
Skipping robust ValidateService checks. Superficial or missing checks can let a broken green environment receive live traffic and require a costly rollback.

screens.title: Canary Deployments
screens.narratorSegment: Canary deployments gradually shift a small portion of production traffic to a new version to test behavior under real load. Start by routing a small percentage — for example 10% — to the canary, monitor metrics like error rates and latency, then increase traffic in steps if metrics remain healthy. CodeDeploy supports canary strategies for Lambda and ECS task sets and integrates with CloudWatch alarms to automate rollback when thresholds are exceeded. A concrete scenario: deploy v2 to a new ECS task set and configure CodeDeploy to shift 10% of traffic for five minutes, then 50% for another period before completing. During these windows, CloudWatch alarms monitoring HTTP 5XX or error rates can trigger a rollback if the canary shows regressions. A typical misconception is to treat the canary window as optional; the canary is only useful if you have meaningful, tightly-scoped alarms and a short observation period that reflects production behavior. Also remember that for stateful changes, canaries may not exercise long-lived sessions fully, so combine canary tests with synthetic checks. When designing alarms, use metrics that indicate user impact and choose thresholds that balance sensitivity and false positives.

keyIdea.title: Canary
keyIdea.text: A staged rollout that shifts small traffic increments and relies on alarms to detect regressions before full rollout.

content.html:
Comparison
Canary Deployment Pattern
Staged traffic shift
Step 1: Shift 10% of traffic and observe for N minutes.
Step 2: If healthy, shift a larger portion, then observe again.
Step 3: Complete rollout when metrics look stable.
Example: ECS service with CodeDeploy moves 10% traffic to a new task set for 5 minutes. CloudWatch alarm monitors 5XX errors. If alarm enters ALARM state, CodeDeploy rolls back to previous task set automatically.
Monitoring tips
  • Monitor error rates, latency, and healthy host counts.
  • Set short evaluation windows during the canary step to reduce exposure time.
  • Use synthetic checks to supplement real-user metrics.
Warning: Canary without alarms provides little protection. The value is in early detection and automated rollback.

screens.title: AppSpec File and Lifecycle Hooks
screens.narratorSegment: The AppSpec file is the blueprint CodeDeploy uses to map files and run lifecycle scripts. It is a YAML file placed at the root of your source bundle. For EC2/on-premises deployments the AppSpec contains fields for version, operating system, files to copy from the revision to the destination, and hooks for lifecycle phases such as BeforeInstall, AfterInstall, ApplicationStop, and ValidateService. A typical ValidateService hook runs a script that calls an HTTP endpoint or runs integration checks. A concrete example is shown in the visual: files mapping copies the artifact into /var/www/html, BeforeInstall installs dependencies, AfterInstall starts the application, and ValidateService performs a curl check that returns a 200 HTTP code. Common mistakes include incorrect YAML indentation or wrong paths for scripts, and scripts that return success prematurely. Ensure scripts are executable and run under the correct user as defined by runas. Also include timeouts to avoid hangs blocking a deployment. The AppSpec is critical because failures here directly cause deployment failure or automatic rollback. When authoring AppSpec hooks, make them idempotent and design ValidateService to fail on any real functional regression so CodeDeploy can protect users.

keyIdea.title: AppSpec
keyIdea.text: A YAML file that maps files and defines lifecycle hooks; robust hooks are critical for safe deployments and rollbacks.

content.html:
Definition
AppSpec Structure & Hooks
Example AppSpec (EC2/on-premises)
version: 0.0
os: linux
files:
  - source: /
    destination: /var/www/html/my-app
hooks:
  BeforeInstall:
    - location: scripts/install_dependencies.sh
      timeout: 300
      runas: root
  AfterInstall:
    - location: scripts/start_application.sh
      timeout: 300
      runas: root
  ApplicationStop:
    - location: scripts/stop_application.sh
      timeout: 60
      runas: root
    - location: scripts/cleanup.sh
      timeout: 60
      runas: root
  ValidateService:
    - location: scripts/validate_service.sh
      timeout: 180
      runas: root
Hook guidance
  • Make hooks idempotent and tolerant to partial state.
  • Set realistic timeouts to avoid stalled deployments.
  • Run ValidateService as a strong end-to-end health check, not a superficial check.
  • Ensure scripts have executable permissions and correct paths.
Key Takeaway

AppSpec defines the deployment contract. Treat it as code: test, lint, and validate hooks before production use.

screens.title: ValidateService Hook — Write Effective Health Checks
screens.narratorSegment: ValidateService is one of the most important lifecycle hooks because a failed validation typically triggers an automated rollback. The goal of a ValidateService script is to verify the application is truly ready to serve production traffic. Good checks exercise real user flows or endpoints: for a web app this means requesting a key A P I route, ensuring authentication works if applicable, and validating response codes and expected payload. Avoid trivial checks that only confirm a process is running; a running process does not imply correct behavior. For example, have your ValidateService check the root HTTP endpoint and parse a known JSON field, then exit with success if the content matches. Include retries with backoff to account for service startup time, and fail fast when a consistent non-200 response appears. Also, log detailed output so agent logs contain actionable diagnostics. A common mistake is overbroad success conditions that mask partial failures. Another pitfall is running ValidateService as an unprivileged user without network access; ensure runas and IAM permissions align with the checks. Closing question: what end-to-end checks will detect the most common failures for your application?

Another pitfall is running ValidateService as an unprivileged user without network access; ensure runas and IAM permissions align with the checks. Closing question: what end-to-end checks will detect the most common failures for your application?

keyIdea.title: ValidateService
keyIdea.text: A robust health check that validates real functionality and triggers rollback when the new version degrades user experience.

content.html:
Core Concept
Designing ValidateService
Best practices
  • Check a real user-facing endpoint and validate the response body.
  • Use retries with exponential backoff during startup windows.
  • Fail explicitly with non-zero exit codes on functional regressions.
  • Emit detailed logs so script failures are diagnosable from agent logs.
Example snippet
A ValidateService script that curls http://localhost, checks for an HTTP 200 code, and optionally verifies a response token or JSON key gives higher confidence than a simple process check.
Common mistake: returning success when the endpoint is reachable but returns an error page. Validate content, not just connectivity.

screens.title: Automated Rollbacks and CloudWatch Integration
screens.narratorSegment: Automated rollbacks are a safety net that revert to the previous healthy version when a deployment fails or when operational metrics degrade. CodeDeploy can automatically rollback when a lifecycle hook exits non-zero or when an associated CloudWatch alarm enters the ALARM state. The typical architecture is: deploy new revision, run ValidateService, monitor CloudWatch metrics linked to the new target or alias, and if alarms trip, CodeDeploy restores traffic to the prior environment or version. For blue/green this means switching the ALB listener back to the blue target group; for Lambda canaries it means reverting the alias to the previous function version; for ECS it means reverting the primary task set. Design your CloudWatch alarms to reflect real user impact — error rates, latency, HTTP 5XX counts, or healthy host counts are good candidates. Avoid overly sensitive alarms that create false positives, but also avoid slow alarms that fail to stop user-facing incidents quickly. A practical example: monitor HTTP 5XX rate with a short evaluation window tied to the canary step. If the alarm triggers, CodeDeploy will roll back automatically, minimizing user exposure. Remember to give alarms appropriate thresholds and to test alarm-triggered rollbacks in a staging environment so you understand the end-to-end behavior.

keyIdea.title: Rollback
keyIdea.text: Use lifecycle-hook failures and CloudWatch alarms as automatic rollback triggers to restore a known good version quickly.

content.html:
Process
Automated Rollbacks
Architecture
Deploy → ValidateService → Monitor CloudWatch alarms → If alarm, trigger rollback. For blue/green, rollback means shifting ALB traffic back to blue. For Lambda canary, revert alias. For ECS, revert task set.
Use error-rate or 5XX metrics for user-visible failures.
Set short evaluation windows during canary steps to shorten exposure.
Test rollback behavior in staging to confirm end-to-end behavior.
Practical checklist
  • Attach CloudWatch alarms to the deployment group and specify thresholds.
  • Ensure CodeDeploy service role has permission to read alarm state.
  • Choose metrics that reflect real user impact, not internal counters only.
Pitfall: alarms that trigger too late or are mis-scoped will not protect users; tune both metric and scope carefully.

screens.title: Troubleshooting CodeDeploy Failures
screens.narratorSegment: Troubleshooting starts with the CodeDeploy deployment timeline in the console. The timeline shows lifecycle hook execution per instance and highlights failures with the failing hook and instance ID. From there, collect the CodeDeploy agent logs and the script output logs on the affected instance. For EC2/on-premises, agent logs reside under /opt/codedeploy-agent/deployment-root/deployment-logs/codedeploy-agent-deployments. log and per-deployment script outputs appear under the deployment group’s deployment folder. These logs contain stderr and stdout from your lifecycle scripts and often include the exact error causing a non-zero exit. Common failure causes include AppSpec syntax errors, missing executable permissions, incorrect script paths, missing dependencies, insufficient IAM permissions for the service role, or network/connectivity problems during validation. For ECS and Lambda, use CloudWatch Logs to capture stdout/stderr and function or task-level logs. A useful workflow: reproduce the failing script locally or in a staging instance, add verbose logging to capture environment variables and command output, then fix the script and re-deploy. Remember to check IAM policies: if CodeDeploy cannot communicate with the compute platform or S3 artifact bucket, deployments will fail before hooks run. When you fix a failure, re-run the deployment to confirm the issue is resolved and inspect the timeline for clean hook execution.

keyIdea.title: Troubleshoot
keyIdea.text: Use the deployment timeline, CodeDeploy agent logs, and CloudWatch Logs to diagnose lifecycle hook failures and configuration errors.

content.html:
Process Flow
Troubleshooting Steps
Step-by-step
  1. Open CodeDeploy console and inspect the deployment timeline for failing hooks and instance IDs.
  2. SSH into affected EC2 instances and open agent logs under /opt/codedeploy-agent/deployment-root/.
  3. Review script stdout/stderr logs in the per-deployment logs folder to see exact errors.
  4. For ECS/Lambda, open CloudWatch Logs for task or function output and inspect recent invocations.
  5. Fix scripts, permissions, or IAM roles, then redeploy in staging before production.
Common root causes
  • AppSpec syntax errors or incorrect file paths.
  • Scripts missing execute permission or incorrect runas user.
  • Missing dependencies or network access for validation steps.
  • Insufficient IAM permissions for CodeDeploy service role.
Pro tip: add verbose logging to ValidateService and capture environment variables to speed diagnosis.

screens.title: Hands-on: Blue/Green Deployment Walkthrough
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on walkthrough ties theory to practice. You will prepare a small Nginx static site and an AppSpec that copies files and runs install and validation scripts. Next, create an Auto Scaling group with instances tagged Environment:Blue and register them with a Blue target group on an ALB. Upload your revision zip to S3 and create a CodeDeploy application and a deployment group initially configured for in-place updates. After verifying app-v1 is served from the ALB, update index. html for v2 and create app-v2. zip. Change the deployment group to blue/green with a GreenTargetGroup and set traffic to reroute immediately. Trigger a deployment of app-v2. Observe CodeDeploy provisioning green instances, running hooks, validating with ValidateService, and rerouting the ALB to green. If validation fails, CodeDeploy will shift traffic back to blue. During this activity, watch the CodeDeploy timeline and instance agent logs to see script output. This exercise demonstrates the end-to-end flow and gives you practice inspecting logs and verifying ALB health checks. After completion, reflect on which ValidateService checks were most effective and whether termination of blue instances should be automated or manual for your environment.

keyIdea.title: Lab
keyIdea.text: Build and deploy a two-version blue/green release to practice AppSpec, ALB target groups, lifecycle hooks, and validation under real conditions.

content.html:
Hands-on Activity
Blue/Green Walkthrough — Lab steps
Starter checklist
  • Create my-web-app with index.html version 1 and an AppSpec at the root.
  • Place scripts/install_nginx.sh, start_nginx.sh, and validate_nginx.sh in scripts/ and make them executable.
  • Zip app-v1.zip and upload to S3, then perform an initial deployment to Blue instances behind an ALB.
  • Update index.html to Version 2, zip app-v2.zip, change deployment group to blue/green, configure GreenTargetGroup, and deploy.
Observe the console timeline as CodeDeploy provisions green instances (or replaces task set), runs install and ValidateService hooks, and reroutes traffic. If ValidateService fails, CodeDeploy will roll back, demonstrating an automated safety net.
Mini-challenge
Modify ValidateService to check a specific HTML token present only in v2. Deploy v2 and observe whether the validation distinguishes the versions as expected.
Key Takeaway

Hands-on practice exposes common pitfalls like missing execute bits, wrong script paths, and insufficient IAM permissions more quickly than theory alone.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: These three concise concepts capture the chapter’s essentials. First, CodeDeploy orchestrates deployments using applications and deployment groups; this mapping determines where revisions go and how they are managed. Second, AppSpec and lifecycle hooks are the deployment contract — they must be written as robust scripts with proper permissions and realistic health checks; ValidateService is your frontline defense. Third, choose a deployment strategy that matches risk and recovery needs: deployment configurations control concurrency, blue/green provides near-zero downtime and instant rollback capability, and canary offers gradual exposure with alarm-driven protection. Practically, always attach meaningful CloudWatch alarms to your rollout and test alarm-triggered rollbacks in staging. When diagnosing failures, rely on the deployment timeline and instance-level agent logs to find failing hooks and script output. Keep these core ideas in mind as you design pipelines: scope targets correctly, write defensive hooks, and let monitoring automate safe rollback decisions. In this lesson you will learn why CodeDeploy is more than a file mover. CodeDeploy is an orchestration engine that coordinates releases across different compute platforms, enforces lifecycle scripts, and integrates automated rollbacks and alarms so you can deploy with confidence. We'll ground the ideas in concrete artifacts: applications, deployment groups, deployment configurations, AppSpec lifecycle hooks, and deployment strategies such as blue/green and canary. You will see the practical tradeoffs: when you need a rapid AllAtOnce push, when to prefer canary testing for live user exposure, and when blue/green is essential to achieve near-zero downtime and instant rollback. We will also cover how to author and validate AppSpec files and how to diagnose failures by inspecting CodeDeploy agent logs and CloudWatch. By the end you should be able to design a deployment group, choose a deployment configuration for your risk profile, and set up alarms and ValidateService hooks that catch real problems before they reach users. Consider what an acceptable rollback trigger looks like for your service and how tests and alarms can be combined to protect production.

By the end of this chapter you will confidently configure CodeDeploy applications and deployment groups across EC2, ECS, Lambda, and on-premises targets. You will be able to author AppSpec files that define file copies and lifecycle hooks, and you will understand how those hooks control deployment flow and automated rollbacks. You will also choose and implement appropriate deployment strategies — AllAtOnce, OneAtATime, HalfAtATime, blue/green, and canary — based on risk, traffic patterns, and the need for zero downtime. Finally, you will set up CloudWatch alarms and interpret CodeDeploy and agent logs to diagnose failures and perform remediations. Each objective focuses on a skill you can immediately apply: configuration, deployment strategy selection, lifecycle scripting, rollback automation, and troubleshooting. For example, you'll practice creating a deployment group that uses tags or an Auto Scaling group to target instances and adding a ValidateService hook that performs a real HTTP health check. Consider which objective will most reduce risk for your next production release and use the lesson that follows to practice that skill.

This lesson emphasizes practical application. You will set up a CodeDeploy application and create a deployment group that targets instances by tag or Auto Scaling group. You will author an AppSpec file that copies files, runs preinstall and validate scripts, and triggers rollback on failures. You will also configure CloudWatch alarms tied to HTTP 5XX rates or latency and link those alarms to CodeDeploy for automatic rollback in blue/green or canary flows. When troubleshooting, you will practice reading the CodeDeploy deployment timeline to identify which hook failed and then examine the CodeDeploy agent logs and script outputs on the instance to find the root cause. These skills are useful immediately: for example, during a release you might deploy a new service to an ECS cluster with canary settings and a CloudWatch alarm for error rate. If error rate rises, CodeDeploy will revert to the previous task set, protecting users. Keep in mind that developing robust ValidateService scripts and correct IAM permissions are the two most common practical blockers. This objective helps you close that gap.

AWS CodeDeploy is a managed service that automates deploying application revisions to a range of compute targets. Think of CodeDeploy as the orchestration layer between your build artifacts and the running instances or services. It stores a revision (for example a zip bundle in S3), maps that revision to an application, and then executes a deployment to a defined set of targets described by a deployment group. In practice, CodeDeploy handles file transfer, lifecycle hooks, traffic shifting for blue/green or canary strategies, and integrates with CloudWatch for automated rollback triggers. A concrete example is deploying a static website bundle to two EC2 instances: CodeDeploy will copy files, run pre- and post-install scripts, and use ValidateService to check the site responds. A common misconception is to treat CodeDeploy only as a file copier; instead, you should treat it as an execution engine that runs your scripts and enforces success criteria. That means well-written lifecycle scripts and correct IAM permissions are critical. Key benefits include repeatability, visibility via the deployment timeline, and safe rollback mechanisms. As you design pipelines, place CodeDeploy after your artifact storage step and before verification and post-deploy tests so it can execute validation hooks and trigger rollbacks when needed. What minimal validation would you include for your next deployment?

At the center of CodeDeploy are two simple concepts: applications and deployment groups. An application is a logical container for your deployment artifacts and configuration. It doesn’t run code itself; instead it groups the deployment groups and the revision history for a particular product or service. A deployment group is where the practical action happens: it defines the set of compute targets that will receive a revision, the deployment configuration to control concurrency, and optional load balancer settings for traffic shifting. Targets are identified differently depending on the platform: EC2/on-premises targets can be selected by instance tags, Auto Scaling group names, or explicit instance IDs; ECS uses a cluster and service; Lambda uses the function name. For example, you might create a deployment group that targets instances tagged Environment:Blue for an in-place update, or create a blue/green group that uses two target groups on an ALB for traffic shifting. A common error is mis-scoping a deployment group: if tags are wrong or IAM roles lack required permissions, CodeDeploy will not find or update targets. The immediate design question is how to scope groups so deployments are predictable and reversible. Think about which selection method — tags, ASG, or explicit IDs — best fits your operational workflow and scaling model.

Deployment configurations determine how many targets are updated simultaneously during a deployment. Choosing the right one balances speed with risk and rollback complexity. The AllAtOnce option updates all targets at the same time. It is fast but risky: a faulty release affects all users immediately. OneAtATime serializes updates so only one instance is changed and validated at a time; this is slow but reduces blast radius and makes troubleshooting simpler. HalfAtATime updates roughly half of instances concurrently, giving a middle ground between speed and safety. When designing your deployment, map your risk tolerance, statefulness, and session handling to a configuration. Stateful services with sticky sessions or long-lived connections may require serial updates or sticky-aware load balancer configurations. For example, an A P I behind an ALB might tolerate HalfAtATime if you have health checks and autoscaling; a database migration that adds incompatible changes would require a OneAtATime or blue/green approach. A frequent misconception is to treat deployment configuration as the only safety control; it must be combined with lifecycle hooks and health checks for meaningful protection. Always test your chosen configuration in a staging environment and measure rollback time for each option so you can quantify the cost of a failed release.

Blue/green deployments isolate the new version in a separate environment, the green environment, while the current production version continues to serve traffic in blue. The process begins by provisioning or identifying replacement targets in the green environment. CodeDeploy deploys the new revision to green and runs all lifecycle hooks, including ValidateService. Once validation passes, you shift traffic from blue to green via the load balancer. If any validation or CloudWatch alarm triggers a failure, you can immediately shift traffic back to blue. For EC2 this often means launching new instances and registering them in the green target group; for ECS it creates a new task set; for Lambda it publishes a new function version and shifts alias routing. Concrete example: with an ALB, configure BlueTargetGroup and GreenTargetGroup, deploy v2 to green, and set the ALB listener to route to green after successful validation. A common mistake is assuming immediate termination of blue instances; unless you explicitly configure termination, retain blue until you're confident. Also, ensure the AppSpec ValidateService hook performs real end-to-end checks so the traffic shift is based on meaningful verification. After a successful shift, you may optionally terminate the blue instances to reclaim resources. What health checks will you run before rerouting traffic?

Canary deployments gradually shift a small portion of production traffic to a new version to test behavior under real load. Start by routing a small percentage — for example 10% — to the canary, monitor metrics like error rates and latency, then increase traffic in steps if metrics remain healthy. CodeDeploy supports canary strategies for Lambda and ECS task sets and integrates with CloudWatch alarms to automate rollback when thresholds are exceeded. A concrete scenario: deploy v2 to a new ECS task set and configure CodeDeploy to shift 10% of traffic for five minutes, then 50% for another period before completing. During these windows, CloudWatch alarms monitoring HTTP 5XX or error rates can trigger a rollback if the canary shows regressions. A typical misconception is to treat the canary window as optional; the canary is only useful if you have meaningful, tightly-scoped alarms and a short observation period that reflects production behavior. Also remember that for stateful changes, canaries may not exercise long-lived sessions fully, so combine canary tests with synthetic checks. When designing alarms, use metrics that indicate user impact and choose thresholds that balance sensitivity and false positives.

The AppSpec file is the blueprint CodeDeploy uses to map files and run lifecycle scripts. It is a YAML file placed at the root of your source bundle. For EC2/on-premises deployments the AppSpec contains fields for version, operating system, files to copy from the revision to the destination, and hooks for lifecycle phases such as BeforeInstall, AfterInstall, ApplicationStop, and ValidateService. A typical ValidateService hook runs a script that calls an HTTP endpoint or runs integration checks. A concrete example is shown in the visual: files mapping copies the artifact into /var/www/html, BeforeInstall installs dependencies, AfterInstall starts the application, and ValidateService performs a curl check that returns a 200 HTTP code. Common mistakes include incorrect YAML indentation or wrong paths for scripts, and scripts that return success prematurely. Ensure scripts are executable and run under the correct user as defined by runas. Also include timeouts to avoid hangs blocking a deployment. The AppSpec is critical because failures here directly cause deployment failure or automatic rollback. When authoring AppSpec hooks, make them idempotent and design ValidateService to fail on any real functional regression so CodeDeploy can protect users.

ValidateService is one of the most important lifecycle hooks because a failed validation typically triggers an automated rollback. The goal of a ValidateService script is to verify the application is truly ready to serve production traffic. Good checks exercise real user flows or endpoints: for a web app this means requesting a key A P I route, ensuring authentication works if applicable, and validating response codes and expected payload. Avoid trivial checks that only confirm a process is running; a running process does not imply correct behavior. For example, have your ValidateService check the root HTTP endpoint and parse a known JSON field, then exit with success if the content matches. Another pitfall is running ValidateService as an unprivileged user without network access; ensure runas and IAM permissions align with the checks. Closing question: what end-to-end checks will detect the most common failures for your application?

When you fix a failure, re-run the deployment to confirm the issue is resolved and inspect the timeline for clean hook execution.

These practices will turn CodeDeploy from a file distribution tool into a robust release orchestration platform that reduces risk and increases deployment confidence. Before your next release, ask: are my hooks meaningful, are alarms tuned, and is my deployment group correctly scoped?
